newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian submarine cable deals to be awarded in March.
newsitem.headline: Asian submarine cable deals to be awarded in March.

text.p: A consortium building the world's longest telecoms submarine cable will award contracts worth over US$300 million for the network's final leg this month, Singapore Telecommunications (SingTel) said on Friday.

Siew Ying Oak, director of submarine cable services at SingTel, told Reuters the contracts would be the last major piece of a global telecoms jigsaw linking four continents and serving half of humanity.

SingTel was one of 86 firms which signed a US$1.3 billion agreement on January 15 to build the new network -- SEA-ME-WE 3 -- which will stretch 38,000 km (23,600 miles) from the South Pacific to the North Atlantic via the Middle East.
The three-leg network will have an initial design capacity of 10 gigabits of data through each of its twin cables, making it four times bigger than previous submarine telecoms cables.
The cable consortium announced $800 million-worth of contracts for the first two stages, between Singapore and Western Europe and between Singapore and Australia in January.
Various other, smaller, contracts for the network have since been awarded separately, analysts say.

Siew, speaking at the launch of a smaller telecoms cable, the Asia Pacific Cable Network (APCN), said contracts for the last leg of SEA-ME-WE 3, from Singapore to various Asian countries, including China and Japan, would be made soon.
"The decision on the award of contracts for the third leg of SEA-ME-WE 3 will be made by the end of this month," Siew said in an interview. "It will be worth more than $300 million."
He said the number of companies receiving contracts to build the Asian leg had not been finally decided and the public announcement of the awards might be made at a later date.

Siew declined to say which companies were in the running for the new contracts. The first two legs are being built by two consortiums which include units of Japan's Kokusai Densin Denwa, Fujitsu and AT&T of the United States.
Siew said the first two stages should be completed by December 1, 1998. The third leg would be ready by March 1, 1999.
"It is usually about two years from the signing of the contract. At the moment that is a target date," he said.
The SEA-ME-WE 3 network consortium includes SingTel, British Telecom, Kokusai Densin Denwa, Deutsche Telekom, Telekom Malaysia, Indosat, France Telecom, Telstra of Australia and China Telecom.
Siew said work on the first two legs of the network was progressing quickly through the initial planning stages.
"For the first two legs of SEA-ME-WE 3, the system design has started but not the factory equipment stage," he said.

The new cables are expected to compete directly with satellites for intercontinental telephone traffic and analysts say they are bound to accelerate the growing price war over global telephone charges.
Siew said the increase in cable capacity brought with SEA-ME-WE 3 would help reduce telephone costs over time.
"When you increase cable capacity it doesn't necessarily mean the cost of calls will go down, but the costs will fall when the number of customers increases and more cables are used," he said.

Announcing the opening of the APCN, SingTel's president and chief executive officer Lee Hsien Yang agreed increased cable capacity would help cut costs, although he said transmission charges represented only part of telephone calling costs.
"We expect the trend of lower costs to continue," Lee told reporters.
